from: a first week in a control room or a van
to: running a team and answering to vendors, carriers and the regulator
case_setting: a named part of the network
series_arc: first week at work → **running a team and speaking for the operator**
learners: They are about to join, or have just joined, a Syrian operator or vendor — where English is the language of the paper trail and of every counterpart abroad: vendor contracts, interconnect and roaming agreements, incident reports, licence conditions, regulatory submissions and settlement files that arrive from eight countries.
neutral: It is **team-neutral within telecoms**. One cohort can contain a control-room engineer, a field technician and a billing analyst, and all three practise the same skill in their own part of the network.
contexts_intro: The programme assumes learners work in different parts of an operator, not one. Twelve telecoms contexts carry the case studies:
upward: **Upward and outward paper:** incident reports, monthly returns, decision papers for a director, claims on carriers and vendors, regulatory submissions and responses to an inspection — usually written, usually read by someone who was not there.
contact: **Vendor and carrier contact:** equipment vendors, foreign carriers, contractors and the regulator, often where neither side is a native speaker.
reading_rows: Tickets, logs, notices, short profiles — 137–190 words
Incident reports, procedures, options papers, breakdowns — 194–287 words
Standards, clauses, submissions, inspection findings — 272–359 words
writing_rows: Notes, slips, logs, a three-line handover — 41–75 words
Decision papers, standards, appraisals, submissions — 147–198 words
move3: Decide, supervise, and speak for the operator
resp2: a site, a figure and a customer
resp2b: a site, a figure and a customer
arc2: someone who owns a site, a figure and a customer
threads: **being honest about what you did not do and cannot evidence** (Course 1 S9 → Course 2 S14 → Course 3 S28); **giving a number its unit, basis and source** (C1 S4 → C2 S16 and S20 → C3 S27); and **writing so that the reader can act** (C1 S12 → C2 S19 → C3 S25).
h1: from your first week in the network to a colleague the shift depends on
h2: from dependable pair of hands to owning a site, a figure and a customer
h3: from owning a site to running a team and answering to vendors, carriers and the regulator
map_example: A learner in the control room meets their own work in sessions 1, 14 and 31, each time at a higher level of responsibility.
posts1: Control-room operator · field technician (towers and power) · service desk agent · fibre and transmission assistant · retail and dealer channel assistant · stores and spares clerk · billing clerk
gives1: Being understood in the control room and on site, taking a fault report accurately, keeping a log a second person can trust, answering for the company on the telephone, holding a safety rule under pressure, accounting for a shift and handing it on
posts2: Shift engineer · site owner in field maintenance · transmission or fibre supervisor · corporate account manager · revenue assurance analyst · dealer channel officer · customer care team leader
gives2: Owning a site and a figure: explaining an outage so a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live equipment, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on a vendor or carrier, recommending with a reservation, and being on the record at the morning meeting
posts3: Operations manager · transmission manager · head of customer care · commercial manager (international) · regulatory affairs manager · security and fraud manager · deputy technical director
gives3: Other people's work and the operator's word: delegating, appraising, chairing an operations review, writing the standard a team follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with vendors and carriers, disagreeing upward, and answering a regulator
constraint: a capable young engineer at the officer grade
sub1: From your first week in the network to a colleague the shift depends on
sub2: From dependable pair of hands to owning a site, a figure and a customer
sub3: From owning a site to running a team and answering to vendors, carriers and the regulator
arc1_text: The learner arrives in a control room or a van unable to operate, and leaves able to be relied on: to take a fault report accurately, keep a log and a register a second person can trust, answer for the company on the telephone, be trusted with site access and spares, hold a safety rule under pressure, account for a shift and hand it on.
arc2_text: The learner is given something of their own — a site, a figure, a customer, a project — and learns the language that ownership requires: explaining an outage so that a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on live equipment, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on a vendor, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen.
arc3_text: The learner becomes answerable for other people's work and for the operator's word. Three sessions are given to supervision itself — delegating, appraising and chairing — and the course runs on through writing the standard a team follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with vendors and carriers, answering a regulator, and arguing for the learner's own next post.
